title: Deadlier germs: do they spread more?
hook: More harm spreads a germ faster but for fewer days. Which harm level spreads it best?

knows: R0: the average number of new cases one carrier causes
doesNotKnow: that harm and spread can pull against each other

misconception: Evolution makes germs either harmless or deadly.
objective: The learner can explain that in a toy where spread rises as the square root of harm while infections shorten as 1 / (1 + harm), R0 is highest at an intermediate harm (v = 1, R0 2.0), not at the lowest or highest.

claims.text: In the trade-off model of virulence, harm that speeds spread also shortens infection, so the strain with the highest R0 can have intermediate virulence.
claims.source: Anderson & May, Coevolution of hosts and parasites, Parasitology 85, 1982; Alizon et al., Virulence evolution and the trade-off hypothesis, J Evol Biol 22, 2009. Both note the theory is debated and real outcomes vary.

claims.text: Toy germ: harm v removes carriers at v per day on top of 1 per day recovery (an infection lasts 1 / (1 + v) days) and spreads 4 x sqrt(v) cases per carrier per day, so R0 = 4 sqrt(v) / (1 + v): 1.6 at v 0.25, 2.0 at v 1, 1.6 at v 4, with its peak at v = 1. At v = 0.25 that is 2.0 cases a day for 0.8 days. The dashed curve on the stage is R0 for every v from 0.1 to 8.
claims.source: Demo.tsx computes rate(v), days(v) and r0(v); grid search in node (artifacts/scratch/w5life/virulence.mjs) peaks at v = 1.00, R0 = 2.000. Other values on the slider: 0.1 gives 1.15, 0.5 gives 1.89, 2 gives 1.89, 8 gives 1.26.

claims.text: Model (stated in the question and reveal): the square-root link between harm and spread is chosen for the toy; real germs vary and the trade-off theory is debated.
claims.source: Model choice in Demo.tsx; brief life #47. Alizon et al. 2009 discuss evidence for and against.

recall.question: In a toy where more harm means faster spread but shorter infections, which germ tends to have the highest R0?
recall.why: R0 is spread rate times infection length. Harm raises the first and cuts the second, so the product peaks in the middle.
